package_info.package_versions: All versions prior to the fix (exact versions not specified)
package_info.why_malicious: The vulnerabilities allowed attackers to publish new versions of any npm package without proper authorization and to leak private package names, both of which could be exploited for supply chain attacks or information disclosure.

execution_context.file_location: npm registry microservices (authorization and publishing services)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During package publishing, the code authorizes the user for one package (from the URL) but publishes a different package (from the uploaded file), allowing unauthorized publishing of arbitrary packages.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This logic flaw allows a user to publish new versions of any npm package, even if they are not authorized for that package.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, publishing a package should require authorization for the specific package being published. Here, the authorization and publishing targets are inconsistent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; package publishing should always be strictly authorized.
key_indicators: Authorization check and publishing action use different package identifiers
Allows privilege escalation to arbitrary package publishing

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During routine maintenance, the code published the names of private npm packages to the public changes feed, exposing private package names to any consumer of the replication server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Private package names are intended to be confidential; exposing them publicly can reveal sensitive project information.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Private package metadata should never be exposed in public feeds.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Publishing public package names is normal, but not private ones.
key_indicators: Private package names appear in public replication feed
No content leaked, but metadata exposure is a breach

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts a publish request with a package file for a target package they do not own, but uses a URL for a package they are authorized for.
attack_chain.leads_to: Unauthorized publishing of a new version of any npm package.

attack_chain.action: During maintenance, private package names are published to the public changes feed.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exposure of private package names to the public.

behavioral_signatures: Discrepancy between package name in authorization and package name in published file
Publishing actions for packages by users not listed as maintainers
Sudden appearance of private package names in public feeds
file_indicators: Records in replicate.npmjs.com containing @owner/package for private packages
Registry logs showing mismatched package names between authorization and publish actions
network_indicators: Unusual publish requests to npm registry with mismatched package identifiers
Access to replicate.npmjs.com with queries for private package names
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm registry logs for publish actions where the authorized user does not match the package being published. Audit the public replication feed for the presence of private package names. Alert on any publish requests or replication feed entries that reference private or unauthorized packages.
